report:
Conclusion: olive leaf extract may modestly lower blood pressure, but the evidence is not strong enough to treat it as a proven antihypertensive or a substitute for prescribed care.

The best human signal comes from small, short trials. A randomized double-blind crossover trial of phenolic-rich olive leaf extract in prehypertensive adults reported improved 24-hour and daytime blood pressure versus control, suggesting a real but modest effect (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5486627/). An earlier open monozygotic-twin study found dose-related reductions with 500–1000 mg/day for 8 weeks, but its open design and tiny sample limit confidence (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/ptr.2455). A double-blind active-controlled trial in stage-1 hypertension reported olive leaf extract performed comparably to captopril over 8 weeks, but it was still small and used a specific extract/dose (https://scholar.ui.ac.id/en/publications/olive-olea-europaea-leaf-extract-effective-in-patients-with-stage/).

Mechanistically, oleuropein/hydroxytyrosol may improve endothelial function, oxidative stress, and vascular tone, which fits the observed BP changes. However, products vary widely in oleuropein content, most studies are underpowered, and long-term outcomes—stroke, heart attack, mortality—are unproven. If someone has hypertension, olive leaf extract should be discussed with a clinician, especially alongside BP medicines, because additive lowering could cause dizziness or hypotension. Lifestyle measures and indicated medications remain the evidence-based foundation.
